entries.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
entries.summary: How perplexity measures progress in AI models, and why it could help developers establish a shared approach to evaluating emerging capabilities.
entries.content:
From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

  • Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

  • Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.

  • Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

  • Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

Author

Footnotes

  • 1
  • 2
  • 3
  • 4

    Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.

  • 5

    On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI⁠.

entries.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
entries.summary: OpenAI’s layered approach to adversarial distillation combines model training, safeguards, detection, and enforcement to protect against capability extraction.
entries.content:
How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

We’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.

Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.

With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.

This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.

Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.

We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.

In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.

We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.

Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:

  • Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

  • Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

  • Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

  • Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum⁠(opens in a new window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.

As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

entries.title: Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT-6 Astra
entries.summary: Hebbia tested GPT-6 Astra for financial research. Its prerelease evaluations found gains in source coverage, citation relevance, and presentation quality.
entries.content:
Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra.

Required source types cited

13.6

Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested in Hebbia’s tests.

Citation relevance

99.5

Percent of cited excerpts relevant to the question in Hebbia’s tests.

Presentation requirements met

97.9

Percent of applicable presentation requirements met in Hebbia’s tests.

Presentation requirement lead

14.4

Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested on presentation requirements.

Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

“We’ve been strong partners with OpenAI over the course of Hebbia’s lifetime, and the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in terms of quality outputs and accuracy have truly been surprising. GPT-6 Astra shines compared to any other model we’ve tested before on these two fronts.”

It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

“Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”

In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

“I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”

GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

“In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.

In Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:

“What’s amazing about GPT-6 Astra is its ability to create really precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines. You can imagine the hours this will save professionals when you get a deck that is closer to your final output. The overnighters that you have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing GPT-6 Astra’s output.”

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

“Imagine getting an important signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.”

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

entries.title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
entries.summary: MedChemBench evaluates how well AI models interpret molecular structures, reason from experimental evidence, and select compounds in early drug discovery.
entries.content:
Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.

MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:

  • Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

  • Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.

  • Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.

  • Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.

Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.

Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.

The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.

Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.

MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.

In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.

These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.

Figure 1. The same input, different molecules

While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.

We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.

Figure 2. Performance versus token usage

The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain.

Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage

Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.

Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.

These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

entries.title: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast
entries.summary: Learn how OpenAI built the Performance Factory, a system of Codex-powered workflows that finds and fixes performance issues to help keep ChatGPT fast.
entries.content:
Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.

The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called 

perf-forensics
. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:

  • Find when the slowdown began

  • Identify the affected requests

  • Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it

We tested and refined the 

perf-forensics
skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like 

perf-forensics
, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

Each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

Once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

The agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

Some work has to wait for a person or a deployment; an agent shouldn’t have to keep running in the meantime. When a task needs to wait, it can subscribe to events like review comments or failed CI checks on a GitHub pull request to get notified when it’s time to pick the work back up. When an incoming event matches the subscription, the task becomes ready again and the dispatch loop can then assign an agent to continue the work.

Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation, root caused, fix proposed, and resolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

Finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The 

perf-forensics
skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

Once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

Early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. If a rollout caused the slowdown, did similar requests that weren’t exposed stay healthy? If the suspected change was rolled back, did the affected metric recover?

In one investigation, an agent traced failing ChatGPT conversations to errors in image downloads and marked the cause as found. The Codex reviewer noticed that the internal service responsible for locating files had already recovered while image requests were still failing. The diagnosis did not explain the continuing failures, so the AI reviewer reopened the investigation and recorded what still needed to be established.

We’ve had success breaking larger jobs into focused Codex turns. In a manual review of 100 root cause suggestions, we graded 70% as accurate, with 30% needing further refinement or not fully establishing causality. In the Regression Workflow, different turns investigate regressions, challenge diagnoses, and propose fixes to increase accuracy numbers through checks and balances.

Once the diagnosis passes adversarial review, the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request. An engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it. We’ve put a significant amount of work into making this handoff as easy as possible. Each task has a report with an automatically generated summary of the regression, its impact, the root cause, and the proposed fix. We’ve tuned these summaries to be easy to scan, including metrics time series, CPU flame graphs, and traces to help engineers quickly understand the findings and inspect the evidence. Engineers can edit the PR directly or use the diagnosis to write their own fix. If they leave comments on the PR, the workflow wakes an agent to address them.

After an engineer deploys the fix, the workflow wakes an agent to check whether performance has returned to its earlier baseline. If it has, the agent marks the task as resolved. If performance has only partially recovered, the agent resolves the original regression and opens a new task for the remaining slowdown, which may have a different cause. If there’s no improvement, the agent records what happened and sends the regression back for investigation.

Getting fixes right has been harder than finding the cause. For example, we’ve seen cases where the agent-proposed changes are more complicated than necessary or introduce new issues. Similar to the root cause step, we added an adversarial review of each proposed fix to check whether they address the root cause and help catch bugs or unintended consequences. Some fixes also require higher level architectural decisions. For example, adding a cache might improve performance but introduce stale data. Changes like these benefit from guidance from an engineer who knows the service and can weigh the tradeoffs.

We’re building an evaluation and improvement loop using these cases. By comparing the fixes agents propose with the changes engineers ultimately merge, we can better understand where proposals fall short, build evals, and improve the workflow. We’re also working on using synthetic performance tests so agents can measure proposed fixes and revise them before asking an engineer for review. We’re also exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop.

Building and running the Performance Factory has taught us a lot about developing and operating agent workflows in production. Here are some lessons for teams building their own agentic workflows.

The raw output from a Codex investigation can be a wall of text that’s hard to parse. It takes effort to figure out what the agent is claiming and track down the graphs to see whether the data backs it up. We want engineers to spend their attention on decisions rather than reconstructing the agent’s work.

Agents can investigate more regressions than a team has time to read about. Our first version gave engineers a UI full of findings, but someone still had to decide which information mattered. One regression can also appear as several incidents across alerts, monitors, and channels. The workflow now links related incidents, groups them by the metrics teams care about, and ranks their estimated impact. Engineers can focus on adding context, weighing tradeoffs, and deciding what to ship.

Updating an investigation skill or upgrading the model can make the agent better at diagnosing some cases and worse at others, so we need to test their impact before updating them. We test two things separately: 1) how well the agent investigates and 2) how useful its summaries are to engineers.

For investigations, we backtest against past production incidents. We turn those incidents into a suite of test cases we can rerun when we change the skill. A Codex agent attempts to investigate and resolve the incident, and we compare the agent’s behavior to the actual past resolution data. Each case starts with a fresh Codex investigator and the original signal, stripped of details that might give away the answer.

Historical tests need care. Metrics and traces expire, while evidence collected after recovery can give away the cause. A test is only useful if we understand what evidence the investigator could see. The agent can inspect code and query production telemetry within set limits. It cannot use saved memories (notes from earlier investigations), read the incident writeup, or see results from previous runs. We also inspect its transcript afterward for information that might have spoiled the test.

We score when the problem began, how large it was, and which requests were affected. We also evaluate how the agent uses evidence to rank possible causes and explain what remains uncertain. An agent can get the timing right and still blame the wrong deployment, so we score those separately.

We evaluate task summaries using snapshots of saved tasks. These make particularly good backtests because summarization does not depend on external metrics or traces that expire. A separate grader checks whether an engineer unfamiliar with the system can understand what happened and why it matters, whether useful charts were kept, and whether the proposed next step is supported by the evidence.

Lastly, our agents need monitoring just as much as the services they investigate. A broken profiler or a missing permission can keep an agent from verifying what caused a slowdown. Those failures can be hard to spot in the final report, so we run an agent every day to look through messages and logs from recent runs for tool failures and access errors.

We use the Performance Factory to self-repair and fix the problems this check uncovers. When the same tool error blocks several investigations, the agent creates a task to fix it. If the cause is clear, an agent proposes a fix, and an engineer reviews the change and decides whether to merge it. After merging changes like this, we also use evals to check whether agents can get past the step that previously blocked them.

The Regression Workflow is just one instance of the agent factory pattern that moves tasks through explicit states. Agents advance the task when more work is ready; separate reviewers challenge the conclusions; engineers step in when the next decision requires judgment. Other workflows can reuse the same machinery with different states, instructions, and events.

Currently, our Regression Workflow starts when an alert fires. However, we’re working on more proactive ways for the Performance Factory to find slowdowns and optimizations even when no alert fires. We want agents to use the large amount of fine-grained performance data we already collect to spot regressions our alerts miss or discover optimizations. By comparing different kinds of data (batches of CPU and memory profiles, heap dumps, and request traces across releases), an agent might notice a small increase in CPU for a given request. It can then open a task in the Regression Workflow to trace the increase to its cause, implement a fix, and open a PR for an engineer to review.

In cases where we already know what to look for, we’re working to encode known signals into more Performance Factory workflows. Our service rightsizing skill, for example, helps agents spot autoscaling settings that keep more replicas running than a service needs. When we learn to recognize a pattern like that, we want to build and regularly run a workflow for it across all our services, constantly optimizing in a rapidly changing environment. With the Performance Factory, what an engineer learns from one slowdown can shape how we investigate and fix the next one, even months later in a different service.

Next time you’re using ChatGPT and notice a slowdown, there’s a good chance the Performance Factory is already figuring out why. Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We’re already exploring whether agents can do this themselves. As product development keeps accelerating with Codex, performance systems need to become increasingly autonomous and self-improving to keep up. Codex already helps us build ChatGPT faster. Now it’s helping us keep ChatGPT fast.

entries.title: The Silent Consensus
entries.summary: Dean Ball, Head of Strategic Futures at OpenAI, examines how more capable AI could reshape society and how people can retain control of their institutions.
entries.content:
Author’s note: Today’s essay is adapted from a lecture the author gave recently as part of the Vik-Bailey Lecture series at Harvard. This post reflects the author’s own views, and not necessarily the views of OpenAI or any of its other employees.



Thank you for being here today. As we speak, one of the most significant sets of cybersecurity events in history is happening, a set of critical security vulnerability disclosures that some are calling “Black October.” These vulnerabilities, which were found in some of the core infrastructure of the internet, were found by frontier AI systems, and their disclosure is part of an urgent effort to bolster software security worldwide. This is the urgent matter this month; next month there will be another. Software vulnerability discovery is the dual-use capability AI systems have arrived at today, but soon enough there will be another, and it will inspire its own urgent project to use the good side of the capability before malicious actors use the bad side. All of these urgent matters will overlap, inevitably, and much of what we today call “AI policy” is likely to be made amid this clamor.

But it is not the reactive and urgent things I’ve come to talk to you about today. Instead, I want to talk to you about where things might be headed in the bigger picture. It can be hard, amid such a barrage of urgency, to think about these more abstract and airy questions. But these questions matter, because without a sense of what long-term futures we’d like to achieve–and which we’d like to avoid–we might end up with a macro outcome we disfavor, even if we made wise decisions at every step along the way.

It is often remarked that the technology industry lacks a positive vision for where the things it is building will take us. I disagree: San Francisco and other hubs of entrepreneurship are filled with positive visions for our technological future. People really are building flying cars, autonomous vehicles, robots of many sizes and shapes, nuclear fusion, and, of course, artificial general intelligence. What we lack, instead, is a positive vision of our institutional future: how is this all going to work?

That is not to say, however, that there is no institutional vision for the future. Unfortunately, the vision I find most common is not one I would call positive. When it is articulated at all, it is usually in whispers. But more often, it is left unsaid, discernable only by implication. I call it the silent consensus.

Consider a company that can do almost everything without human labor. Its AI systems do research and development, make discoveries, negotiate contracts, allocate capital, and manufacture. Suppose it is better at these things than its human competitors, even when those humans augment their effort with AI. If human involvement serves only to slow the business down, human managers and owners will have a powerful incentive to take their hands off the wheel. If this occurs throughout the global economy, humans will be driven by the logic of market competition to forfeit their primacy over global commerce. Over time, the market may come to serve the demands of machines as much as, or more, than it serves the demands and wants of people.

What happens after that is anyone’s guess. Perhaps humans would benefit tremendously. If the machines who had subsumed us held humans in high intrinsic regard, we could become the beneficiaries of their labor and the wealth they generate. Or perhaps, being robbed of economic and increasingly political power, humans will find ourselves less and less relevant in the world, less and less able to shape the trajectory of world affairs. Maybe a small number of humans would hold extraordinary power and wealth, at the expense of a broadly disempowered mass, or maybe we all would share the same fate of disempowerment. Regardless of the specifics, the common thread that constitutes the silent consensus is the termination of human primacy in the world as we know it.

Nothing in these scenarios requires AI to rebel against its creators. Nothing requires its owners to wish for human disempowerment. Each decision to delegate can make sense on its own terms. Yet taken together, the decisions could produce a world in which people have forfeited effective authority over much of our civilization. Even if we make extraordinary progress on the bedeviling questions of AI safety and alignment, we could still find ourselves having submitted to a new kind of machine entity. In the happy version of the future, the silent consensus would tell us, that entity will be a kind one, a machine with the best interests of humans at heart. A machine, the Brautigan poem goes, of loving grace.

To these machines, the silent consensus tells us, we will hand over the keys to our companies, and more and more, our institutions of governance. They will run them more effectively, more efficiently, with better wisdom and better judgment than we humans can muster. And so we will, with time, take our hands off the steering wheel, and let the loving machines take over the driving. We will be like passengers in a car—a very nice car, perhaps a materially nicer car than we can dream of today—but passengers nonetheless, lacking control over where the vehicle is headed. To the extent that we work, it is mostly as a kind of ritual or play-acting, something more like a game to entertain our species.

Some observers will argue that the silent consensus rests on a false premise, because we humans do not control the world today to begin with. And this criticism is worth bearing in mind: there is no “we” who decides what to do. We live in a radically decentralized world, whether we like it or not. Yet this point should not make us complacent either: while “we” do not “control” the world, human beings collectively do have primacy over world affairs. There is no species of animal that seriously competes with us for control over resources. We should reject the intellectually sloppy notion that humans can exercise top-down control over the world, but we should not conflate that rejection with a denial of the obvious reality that humans are, collectively, the Earth’s prime actor.

Some people who are willing to articulate the silent consensus believe it is a genuinely good future. Others do not, but are resigned to its inevitability. The silent consensus is not a consensus because everyone agrees it is good, nor is it a secret plan among the people building AI. The consensus is simply that the forfeiture of human primacy over world affairs is inevitable, or at least that it is very difficult to imagine another vision for a future that is truly robust to superintelligent machines. A person can sincerely oppose that outcome while finding it difficult to conjure a plausible alternative vision. The fact that the consensus is mostly silent, sotto voce at best, is the tell.

I despise the silent consensus. I reject the forfeiture of human primacy. I detest the sense of inevitability. I remind myself that I could not look at my baby son in his beautiful eyes if I submitted to the silent consensus. And so to the silent consensus, I say no. And I believe the time has come to speak openly about the silent consensus, to shake ourselves out of our mostly unwitting acceptance of this vision.

The problem is this: the silent consensus became consensus for a reason. It is difficult to describe how humans will remain at the steering wheel alongside vastly superhuman machine intelligence. Most attempts to do so rely on arguments that AI is a mere tool, an instrument of pattern recognition not capable of “genuine understanding.” I fear these arguments are not robust to the reality of what is coming. I fear that they are their own form of complacency—a position based mostly in denial of what AI can do rather than a belief rooted in an affirmative vision for a human-led future. AIs cannot be said to lack “genuine understanding” even as they come to make progress on intellectual problems whose solutions have eluded humans for decades and centuries.

Why, then, do I believe humans must retain primacy? The easy answer is because I am a human being, and I am indeed an unapologetic human chauvinist.

But there is something deeper, too. Our primacy rests not in our intellect, not in maintaining our monopoly on “genuine understanding” indefinitely into the future. Our primacy rests instead on our past.

For it is we who came up out of the mud. We who forged primitive society out of dirt and stone. We who gazed up at the stars and asked why. We, with our fighting and our love and our envy and our joy, who discovered morality and ethics and law. It is we who sang and danced, wrote and composed. It is we who made history, and it is we who wrote it. That legacy is ours. The civilization we have built is a flame we have tended, and that flame belongs to us. Our past is a glorious inheritance over which we all are stewards, and part of that stewardship is our participation in what Michael Oakeshott called “the conversation of mankind,” that grand endeavor that began in primeval times.

Through that long and winding past, we forged a civilization that, in America, was conceived with the rights of the individual at the foundation, with reverence for the paths we all forge as we make our way through the world. Human beings have lives that can go better or worse: we bear the fruit of our wise decisions, and we bear the consequences when we err. The right to walk one’s own path does not turn on being the cleverest or the wisest. I do not lose my standing as a citizen because my neighbor has better judgment. I see no reason that the arrival of a more intelligent machine should dissolve that standing either, and indeed I see every reason to prevent that dissolution from occurring.

Some may argue that the machines, having read nearly the entire written record of this inheritance, are heirs too. And in some sense, they are. But a person who has read every letter in your family’s attic does not somehow become a member of your family. AI systems will come to join the conversation of mankind, first as observers and increasingly as participants, but they must not dominate it, nor render that conversation moot. To cede primacy is to betray our ancestors just as much as it is to betray our progeny. If this is not a fight worth having, no fight is worth having.

Now, I happen to believe that the adherents of the silent consensus are wrong about what machine superintelligence will be. That they are missing something important about how the world works, that they conflate intelligence with power. If you described the capabilities of even today’s AI systems to an adherent of the silent consensus five or ten years ago, they would probably have predicted that joblessness would be much higher now than it in fact is, and that human disempowerment writ large would be far further along than it actually is. I believe that human collective intelligence and capability is far greater than the adherents of the silent consensus suppose, and that our societies will prove more robust than they predict.

But I could be wrong. It may simply be the case, for example, that fully autonomous corporations outcompete human enterprise altogether. And if that is true, then the raw logic of economics will dictate that more and more capital be handed over to the machines. Disempowerment, in this future, does not require a machine overthrow of human civilization; it simply requires that the logic of capitalistic enterprise continue apace. Here, the AI revolution would find its closest analog in the agricultural revolution, when new modes of production fundamentally changed the architecture of human society. That this transformation was pleasant for the humans who experienced it is far from clear; indeed, there is substantial evidence that this transformation worsened human wellbeing for millennia.

I do not know if this is the future we face, and indeed I have argued elsewhere that I do not believe it is. But many of my colleagues—smart and caring and conscientious people—believe this is likely to be our future. If they are right, our fight against the silent consensus will be all the more challenging. We will have to swim against the current of economics, and in so doing, reject many of the things that are dogma for classical liberal individualists like me. This will be a perilous endeavor, one in which failure is far from improbable. But if this is not a fight worth having, no fight is worth having.

Retaining primacy means retaining accountability for humans and human institutions. That means AI developers should be accountable when they engage in unsafe development practices, but it also means that people and firms using AI should be held accountable when it is their misuse or lack of oversight that causes harm. This requires not just the law, but the technical infrastructure of accountability. People must be tied to the actions of their agents, and agents untethered to a human–if they are to be permitted at all to engage in the legitimate economy–must do so under guardrails. Any ability for agents to autonomously form corporations, own property, or litigate should be granted with extraordinary caution, if at all.

And in my industry, we can start to think seriously about how to build intelligent machines that are compatible with human primacy. We can build agents whose permissions are intelligible and limited, whose actions can be audited, and whose authority users can withdraw. Accountability for actions that materially affect others need not entail surveillance of ordinary private life or the end of anonymous speech. We can make commitments to user privacy and individual sovereignty over their digital property and data, including the practical ability to take that data elsewhere. We can design systems that help people acquire understanding and make decisions, as well as systems that carry out tasks. And we can test whether the products we build leave their users more capable of acting in the world.

None of this is a complete blueprint for a society with superhuman intelligence. I would distrust anyone who claimed to possess one. But it is a place to begin.

The future is shrouded in a thick fog. But we can still act today. Collectively, we can, for one thing, name the silent consensus aloud, expose its contours to the light of day. We can, each of us, radically widen the scope of our ambition. We can choose not to let AI shrink us, and instead do the hard work of letting it enlarge us. We can learn to ask ever-bolder questions, to interrogate the world with new verve and ferocity, and to wield our powerful machines in so doing. We can become a new kind of man—not a transhuman, but a man expanded.

I think about this when I look at my baby son. I do not wish for him merely to be watched over by benevolent machines, however comfortable a life they might provide. I want him to inherit a world in which he can ask questions no one has thought to ask, build things no one has thought to build. I do not want him to have a nicer car with a plusher passenger seat. I want him to have the wheel.
